title: Decode slab heuristics — field notes and micro-benchmarks
content:
Purpose:
Quick internal write-up of an exploratory micro-benchmark comparing two decode strategies we prototyped: 'slabification' (chunked decode that emits partial tokens earlier by interleaving token slices) vs full-frame decode (standard left-to-right). Goal: surface latency tail behavior, downstream token-throughput, and rough $/token impact for different GPUs and batch shapes. These are early field notes — not polished; recording commands, raw numbers, and open questions for follow-up experiments.

Test harness and environment:
- Code: branch slab-proto-6 (rtengine) local runner + synthetic client harness. See PR in linked_artifacts.
- Models: open-7b-compat quantized 4-bit / baseline fp16 variant.
- Datasets/workloads: synth-conv-1k (short convo-like prompts, avg prompt len 64 tokens, gen target 128 tokens), long-tail-wiki (avg prompt 320, gen 256), ravenbench-v2 interleaved bursts.
- Hardware: A100-40GB (core rack), H100-80GB (prod-reef), T4-sim (cheap baseline for batch shapes).
- Measurement: p50/p95/p99 latency for first-token and tail-token; tokens/sec aggregate; approximate infra $ calculated using on-demand vGPU hourly rate mapping.
- Client shape: steady arrival (Poisson lambda tuned) + synthetic spike windows to stress tail.

Experiment variations (key knobs):
- Mode A: full-frame decode (baseline).
- Mode B: slabification chunk size = 16 tokens (emit partial token groups as they complete).
- Batch shapes: concurrency (C) x batch (B) = CxB where we drove the server via multiple clients; we report logical 'effective batch' equivalent for the model run. Example shapes tested: 1x1, 1x4, 4x8, 8x16.
- KV-caching: on for repeated session runs (where applicable) vs cold for first session.

Representative numeric summary (synth-conv-1k, open-7b-compat fp16, A100) — numbers are medians of 3 runs, p95/p99 are empirical

Mode | Batch | 1st-token p50(ms) | 1st-token p95(ms) | tail p50(ms) | tail p95(ms) | tokens/sec | ~$ per 1M tokens
-----|-------|-------------------:|-------------------:|--------------:|--------------:|-----------:|-----------------:
Full | 1x1   | 46                | 132               | 390          | 920          | 1,150      | 13.7
Full | 1x4   | 60                | 180               | 420          | 1,050        | 3,800      | 8.9
Full | 4x8   | 78                | 260               | 540          | 1,600        | 11,200     | 3.1
Slab | 1x1   | 32                | 88                | 360          | 760          | 1,350      | 11.6
Slab | 1x4   | 38                | 110               | 390          | 820          | 4,200      | 7.4
Slab | 4x8   | 55                | 170               | 500          | 1,100        | 12,600     | 2.8

Quick interpretation: slabification reduces first-token latency across the board (notably at low concurrency) and tightens p95 for first-token by ~25–35% vs full-frame. Tail token improvements are smaller; slab helps to shift some token emission earlier but overall end-to-end generation time (tail p95) still dominated by compute for long outputs. Aggregate tokens/sec improves modestly in mixed shapes (1x4/4x8) because earlier token emission allows better client-side pipelining. Estimated $/1M tokens shows 10–20% savings for synthetic short convo workload at low concurrency, tapering as we scale to high batch occupancy where full-frame batching wins on pure throughput.

ASCII micro-trace (single-run p90 series for a 128-token generation, 1x4, A100):
Time(ms) 	 Full-frame emit timeline (token index emitted)
0    	 [req received]
46   	 token-0 (client sees first token)
140  	 token-30
280  	 token-70
420  	 token-110
560  	 token-127 (done)

Time(ms) 	 Slabified emit timeline (chunk=16)
0    	 [req received]
32   	 token-0
90   	 token-16
170  	 token-48
260  	 token-96
360  	 token-127 (done)

The slab trace shows earlier steady trickle of content which is good for UX streaming and reduces perceived latency even when total compute is similar.

H100 vs A100 spot check (synth-conv-1k, 1x1):
- H100 full-frame first-token p50 34ms, p95 94ms; slab first-token p50 24ms, p95 62ms.
- H100 tokens/sec ~1.6x A100 for same build; $/1M tokens roughly 0.9x depending on instance price — so H100 dominance improves both latency and unit cost for steady throughput.

T4 sim (cheap baseline) shows slab gives disproportionate UX improvements at tiny batches but total throughput still limited. Not a target for high-SLA customers, but useful for dev/low-cost regions.

Spike window behavior (short 10s burst at 3x baseline):
- Full-frame: p99 tail jumps badly (2–3x baseline) and queueing increases; slab shows smoother p99 increase because early emission frees NVLink/PCIe stalls earlier for downstream components.

Open questions and caveats:
- Memory pressure: slab increases ephemeral activation footprint slightly for some quantized kernels — saw a few OOMs on dense 80-token context runs; need deeper kernel-level accounting.
- Determinism and alignment: slab breaks strict token-alignment expected by some redispatch heuristics (we need to validate function-calling and deterministic sampling behavior under slab).
- Cost calc approximations: we used on-demand vGPU rates and ignored amortized infra costs (storage, control plane). Also model quantization candidate plays a big role — fp16 vs 4-bit changed tokens/sec by 1.6x in our runs.
- Client/SDK changes: to realize UX gains we need SDK stream APIs to accept partial-chunk frames; current SDK requires small protocol changes and back-compat.

Recommendations (next steps):
1) Run full matrix across (A100,H100) x (fp16,4-bit) x (chunk sizes 8,16,32) focusing p99 first-token and tail p95.
2) Add memory profiling hooks inside runtime to capture ephemeral mem per-slab step.
3) Re-run with real-world prompt mix (prod-sampled sessions) to validate $/token shifts.
4) Spike testing with our admission controller enabled to see how slab interacts with slotization and pacing.
5) Draft SDK streaming compatibility changes (small) and document backward compatibility.

Commands used (example):
- ./bench/run_client.sh --model open-7b-compat --mode slab --chunk 16 --clients 4 --promptset synth-conv-1k --gpu a100
- ./bench/collect.sh --tag slab-16-a100-20290615 > results/slab-16-a100-20290615.json

Notes for the product/marketing collateral team:
- UX takeaway: slabification provides earlier streaming tokens (perceived latency improvement) while generally preserving or slightly improving total throughput for typical convo workloads. This is a clean story for ‘streaming-first’ experiences where per-token stagger matters.
- Caution: not a one-size-fits-all optimization — for purely batch-bounded throughput (high sustained multiplexing), standard batching still edges out in pure $/token.

Appendix — raw p99 scatter (1x4, 128 gen, A100, three runs):
RunID    | Mode   | 1st-token p99(ms) | tail p99(ms)
r1       | full   | 185              | 1040
r2       | full   | 172              | 980
r3       | full   | 190              | 1105
r1       | slab   | 112              | 870
r2       | slab   | 118              | 820
r3       | slab   | 125              | 910

Open items for discussion at next sync (agenda bullets):
- Kernel memory accounting: who owns adding counters? (platform-engineering)
- SDK streaming wire protocol changes (devx + console)
- Prioritize slab experiments across quantization matrix (research + serving-runtime)

Bottom line (summary sentence):
Slabification (chunked early-emits) looks promising for improving perceived latency and tightening first-token tails with modest or neutral impact on throughput and unit cost for convo-style workloads; we should pursue a targeted experiment plan and add runtime memory counters before recommending wider rollout.

-- Ava
